families.title: Corners
families.mathematics: Corners of regular polygons with the same side fit round a point side to side: a triangle’s corner is 60°, a square’s 90° and a pentagon’s 108°. Three or more fold into a pointed corner with no dent exactly when they make less than a whole turn (each angle is then less than the others together, so the corner exists); they lie flat at exactly a whole turn and overlap past it. The missing part of the turn is the corner’s gap. Up to turning and flipping, 11 rings of triangles and squares fold to a point (from 10 sets of corners) and 4 lie flat; pentagons add 14 pointed rings and no flat one. With some corners fixed, some filling of the free places folds exactly when the filling with the smallest corner everywhere folds, so that ring laid flat is the proof that none does. An opened drawing is a convex solid seen through one face that has been taken out: a connected plane drawing whose closed regions are the other faces. Erasing a line with different spaces on its two sides keeps every dot joined and removes one region; erasing a line with the same space on both sides cuts the drawing. A tree has one line fewer than dots (taking off an end dot with its one line leaves a tree, down to one dot), so erasing down to one takes one erasure per region and dots − lines + regions = 1 throughout: V − E + F = 2 on the solid.
rules: Corners of triangles, squares and pentagons, all with the same side, lie flat round the point, side to side, in the order they are added.
Fold joins the first corner’s free side to the last one’s. The corners fold to a point, lie flat or overlap.
A ring read from another corner, or the other way round, is the same ring.

parent.notice: Whether your child predicts the fold before pressing it, and whether they connect a folded ring with a corner of a paper solid.
parent.prompt: Can you build the corner of the square pyramid’s top? Of its base?
parent.explanation: The pyramid’s top has four triangles (240°) and each base corner a square and two triangles (210°). Rings fold to a point under 360°, lie flat at 360° and overlap past it.
parent.extension: Build every corner of one paper solid and add up the gaps. (Always 720°, Descartes’ theorem; Problem 4.)
parent.connection: Week 56 Problems 3, 4 and 5: corners of the paper solids and their gaps.

puzzles.idea: Triangle corners fold to a point while they leave a gap: three, four or five of them. Six make a whole turn and lie flat.
puzzles.prerequisites: Tell triangles, squares and pentagons apart and see whether corners leave a gap. No reading; a grown-up can read How to play.
hints: Add triangle corners one at a time and press Fold each time. When do they stop folding to a point?
Three, four and five triangle corners leave a gap and fold. Six make a whole turn and lie flat; seven overlap.
Keep the rings of three, four and five triangles, then press That’s all.

parent.notice: Whether your child adds one more triangle each time and watches the gap shrink, and whether they try six and seven.
parent.prompt: What happens to the gap when you add a triangle?
parent.explanation: Each triangle corner is 60°, a sixth of a turn. Three, four and five make 180°, 240° and 300°, leaving gaps of 180°, 120° and 60°, so they fold into the corners of the tetrahedron, the octahedron and the icosahedron. Six make exactly 360° and lie flat, like the triangles of a floor tiling; seven overlap.
parent.extension: Which solids have three, four and five triangles at every corner? (The tetrahedron, the octahedron and the icosahedron.)
parent.connection: A corner of a convex solid needs its face angles to add to less than a whole turn; the gap is its angular defect.

puzzles.idea: Three squares leave a quarter turn; only a corner smaller than a square fits in it and still folds.
puzzles.prerequisites: Fold a ring and see whether it overlaps, lies flat or leaves a gap. The hints use degrees (60, 90 and 108).

parent.notice: Whether your child tries all three shapes, and what they expect a fourth square to do.
parent.prompt: Why does a fourth square lie flat?
parent.explanation: Three squares make 270°. A triangle brings the total to 330° and the corner folds; a square makes 360° and lies flat; a pentagon makes 378° and overlaps.
parent.extension: Three squares alone fold too: that is a cube’s corner. Which solid has three squares and a triangle at every corner? (The small rhombicuboctahedron.)
parent.connection: Corners with more than one kind of face belong to the Archimedean solids.

puzzles.idea: Any three squares and pentagons leave a gap, and any four overlap or lie flat, so the rings are the four ways to choose three.
puzzles.prerequisites: Tell triangles, squares and pentagons apart and see whether corners leave a gap. No reading; a grown-up can read How to play.
hints: Fold rings of three corners, then rings of four.
Every ring of three folds. Four squares make a whole turn already, and a pentagon is bigger than a square.
Keep three squares, two squares and a pentagon, a square and two pentagons, and three pentagons. Then press That’s all.

parent.notice: Whether your child tries four corners and sees that they never fold, and whether they notice that two squares and a pentagon is one ring however it is turned.
parent.prompt: Why can’t a ring have four of these corners?
parent.explanation: The smallest four are four squares, 360°, which lie flat; any pentagon makes more. Every three fold: the biggest, three pentagons, make 324°. That gives SSS, SSP, SPP and PPP, and with three corners every order is the same ring.
parent.extension: Which solid has three pentagons at every corner? (The dodecahedron.) Is there a solid with a square and two pentagons at every corner? (No: round each pentagon its neighbours would have to alternate between squares and pentagons, and five is odd.)
parent.connection: Three pentagons at a corner build the dodecahedron (Problem 9’s second picture).

puzzles.idea: Three triangle corners fill the same turn as two squares, so a flat ring trades squares for triangles; two squares with three triangles go round in two different orders.
puzzles.prerequisites: See when two rings are the same after turning or flipping, and keep track of the shelf. The hints use degrees (60, 90 and 108); a grown-up can read How to play.
hints: Fold rings until one lies flat. Can you swap some of its corners for others and still lie flat?
Three triangle corners make 180°, the same as two squares. Four squares, two squares with three triangles, and six triangles all make a whole turn.
Two squares and three triangles go round in two ways: the squares side by side, or with a triangle between them. Keep all four rings, then press That’s all.

parent.notice: Whether your child finds the trade of two squares for three triangles, and whether they find the second order.
parent.prompt: Are the squares side by side in every flat ring with two squares?
parent.explanation: A flat ring makes 360°: 90 × squares + 60 × triangles = 360 gives four squares, two squares and three triangles, or six triangles. Two squares and three triangles can be round the point with the squares touching or with one triangle between them (the other side then has two), and no turning or flipping takes one to the other.
parent.extension: Each flat ring tiles a floor round one point. Which of them tile the whole floor with every point alike? (All four.)
parent.connection: These are the vertex types of the regular and semiregular tilings made of squares and triangles.

puzzles.provenance: Week 56 Grades 2–5 Problem 3 (“Which close flat with no gap?”) widened to mixed rings, as the card’s second run counts them (SSSS, TTTTTT, TTTSS, TTSTS).

puzzles.idea: A flat ring makes a whole turn exactly. Two triangles leave 240°: three more triangles fall short and fold up, three squares go past, and two squares with a triangle fill it, so the smallest corners everywhere are not the answer here.
puzzles.prerequisites: Fold a ring and see whether it overlaps, lies flat or leaves a gap. The hints use degrees (60, 90 and 108).
hints: Fill the three places and press Fold. Does the ring fold up, lie flat or overlap?
Two triangles make 120°, so the other three corners must make exactly 240°. Three triangles make 180°, and each square in place of a triangle adds 30°.
Two squares and a triangle make 240°. Add them and press Fold.

parent.notice: Whether your child changes one corner at a time after a fold, and in which direction: a ring that folds up needs a bigger corner, one that overlaps a smaller one.
parent.prompt: The ring folded up. Which corner would you make bigger?
parent.explanation: Two triangle corners make 120°, so the three free corners must make exactly 240° for the ring to lie flat. Three triangles make 180° and fold up; each square in place of a triangle adds 30°, so two squares and a triangle make 240°. A pentagon never fits: with one, the other two would need 132°, and two of 60° and 90° make 120°, 150° or 180°. The smallest corners everywhere fold to a point, so in this puzzle the smallest filling is not the answer.
parent.extension: The three free corners go in three orders. Which of the rings you get are the same ring? (Triangle, triangle, square, square, triangle and triangle, triangle, triangle, square, square are one ring, with the squares side by side; triangle, triangle, square, triangle, square has a triangle between the squares. These are the two orders in Rings 4.)
parent.connection: Flat rings are the corners of floor tilings by squares and triangles; Rings 4 finds them all.

A bigger corner only adds more, so no ring like this folds to a point. Fold two squares and three triangles, then press Can’t.

parent.notice: Whether your child tries smaller corners after a fold that overlaps, and whether they can say why one ring settles every other.
parent.prompt: How do you know no other filling works?
parent.explanation: Two squares make 180°. Three more corners are at least three triangles, 180°, so every filling makes at least 360°: the smallest lies flat and every other overlaps. Folding the smallest is the proof.
parent.extension: With four places instead of five, which fillings fold? (A triangle with a triangle, a square or a pentagon: 300°, 330° and 348°.)
parent.connection: A bound by the smallest case: if the best case fails, every case fails.

puzzles.idea: Five corners fit in a turn only with four triangles; the fifth can be any shape.
puzzles.prerequisites: See when two rings are the same after turning or flipping, and keep track of the shelf. The hints use degrees (60, 90 and 108); a grown-up can read How to play.
hints: Fill the five places and press Fold. Which corners leave room for five?
Five triangles make 300°. Swapping one triangle for a square or a pentagon still leaves a gap; swapping two never does.
Keep five triangles, four triangles with a square, and four triangles with a pentagon. Then press That’s all.

parent.notice: Whether your child starts from five triangles and swaps, and whether they check two swaps.
parent.prompt: Why can only one corner be something other than a triangle?
parent.explanation: Five triangles make 300°. Swapping one triangle for a square adds 30° (330°) and for a pentagon 48° (348°): both fold. Two swaps add at least 60°, to 360° or more. With one odd corner, every order is the same ring.
parent.extension: Which solid has five triangles at every corner? Four triangles and a pentagon? (The icosahedron; the snub dodecahedron.)
parent.connection: The snub cube (four triangles and a square) and the snub dodecahedron are the two snub Archimedean solids.

parent.notice: Whether your child fills with squares after seeing pentagons overlap.
parent.prompt: Would it help to put the pentagon somewhere else in the ring?
parent.explanation: A pentagon is 108° and a square 90°, so a pentagon and three squares make 378°. Every other filling has more pentagons and more degrees. The order round the point never changes the total.
parent.extension: With triangles offered too, which fillings fold? (Three triangles; two triangles with a square or a pentagon; a triangle and two squares: 288°, 318°, 336° and 348°.)
parent.connection: Only the total decides whether corners fold to a point; their order decides which ring it is.

puzzles.idea: Sort the rings by how many corners they have: four of three, five of four (two squares and two triangles go round two ways) and two of five.
puzzles.prerequisites: See when two rings are the same after turning or flipping, and keep track of the shelf. The hints use degrees (60, 90 and 108); a grown-up can read How to play.
hints: Sort rings by how many corners they have. Which rings of three fold to a point?
Every ring of three folds. Four corners fold unless all four are squares; five fold only with at most one square.
Two squares and two triangles go round in two ways: squares side by side, or opposite. That makes 4 rings of three, 5 of four and 2 of five. Keep all 11, then press That’s all.

parent.notice: Whether your child organises the search by size or by number of squares, and how they spot that a ring is already on the shelf.
parent.prompt: Is two squares and two triangles one ring or two?
parent.explanation: Three corners: SSS, SST, STT, TTT (270° at most). Four: TTTT, STTT, SSTT, STST, SSST (330° at most; SSSS lies flat). Five: TTTTT and STTTT (330°); SSTTT lies flat. Six or more make at least 360°. That is 11 rings from 10 sets of corners, since two squares and two triangles can be side by side or opposite.
parent.extension: Which of these are the corner of a solid with every corner alike? (All but two: TTT, TTTT, TTTTT, SSS, SST, STTT, SSST, STST and STTTT are the corners of the tetrahedron, octahedron, icosahedron, cube, triangular prism, square antiprism, small rhombicuboctahedron, cuboctahedron and snub cube. STT and SSTT are not: round a triangle the neighbours would have to alternate between triangles and squares.)
parent.connection: Corners with a positive gap; the card’s second run finds 11 rings from 10 piece sets.

parent.notice: Whether your child checks that every dot is still joined after an erasure.
parent.prompt: How many lines did you erase, and how many shaded regions were there?
parent.explanation: The tetrahedron has 4 corners, 6 edges and 4 faces; seen through one face, its drawing has 4 dots, 6 lines and 3 shaded regions. Each line erased on a loop takes away one line and one region. After three, 4 dots and 3 lines are left with no region: a tree. So dots − lines + regions is 1, and with the missing face back V − E + F = 2.
parent.extension: Erase a different three lines that also leave a tree. How many ways are there? (Sixteen of the twenty ways to choose three lines; the other four leave a triangle and a lone dot.)
parent.connection: Neale’s edge-removal proof of Euler’s formula (NRICH).

parent.notice: Whether your child erases both halves of the bottom side and sees the dot between them cut off, and whether they peel from the outside or erase inner lines first.
parent.prompt: The extra dot brought one more dot and one more line. Did it change how many lines you erased?
parent.explanation: Problem 6 puts a dot along one edge of the cube: 9 corners, 13 edges and 6 faces, still V − E + F = 2. Seen through one face, that is 9 dots, 13 lines and 5 shaded regions. A line with different spaces on its sides lies on a loop: erasing it joins the two spaces, so one region goes and every dot stays joined. The new dot has two lines on the same loop; once one is erased, the other is the only way to that dot. A tree on 9 dots has 8 lines, so 5 erasures are needed, one per region, and 9 − 13 + 5 = 1 throughout. Guide p. 7’s route (AB, BC, CD, DA, then ab) works with one half of AB.
parent.extension: Erase only inner lines first. Does it still take five erasures? (Yes: every erasure on a loop removes one region, whichever two spaces it joins.)
parent.connection: Redrawing a surface changes its counts but not V − E + F (Problem 6); the erasures explain why, for every drawing.

parent.notice: Whether your child keeps track of which dots are still joined as the drawing thins out, and whether they see that an end dot always comes off with exactly one line.
parent.prompt: When you take off an end dot, what happens to the dots and the lines?
parent.explanation: The octahedron has 6 corners, 12 edges and 8 faces; seen through one face, 6 dots, 12 lines and 7 shaded regions. Seven erasures, one per region, leave a tree with 5 lines. Taking off an end dot takes one dot and one line and leaves a tree, so dots and lines go down together until 1 dot and no line are left: a tree has one line fewer than dots. No step changes dots − lines + regions: 6 − 12 + 7 = 1 at the start and 1 − 0 + 0 = 1 at the end. With the missing face back, V − E + F = 2 (guide p. 7).
parent.extension: Why is there always an end dot to take off? (Walk along the tree’s lines without going back. With no loop you never come back to a dot, so the walk has to stop, and it stops at an end dot.) Can a tree keep all three outside lines? (No: they make a loop.)
parent.connection: Guide p. 7’s leaf argument for E = V − 1, on the drawing the card’s fix 3 adds.
